content.text:
I submitted the verdict **holistic**, with confidence 0.88. I used 22 of the 60 budget: 1 training run and 21 tests.

**Design:** I trained the learner on one task, L1-S1-M1. I then tested tasks that differ from it in which rules are new, using the free `compare` command to measure how much each one's outputs overlap with the trained task. Under the part-based hypothesis, tasks with the same number of new rules should cost about the same.

| Test task | New rules | Output overlap with trained task | Examples to criterion | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M2 | 1 (motor) | 0.75 | 7, 4, 1, 20, 1 | ~7 |
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 (motor) | 0 | 60, 25, 32 | ~39 |
| L2-S1-M1 | 1 (logic) | 0 | 26, 34, 35 | ~32 |
| L1-S2-M1 | 1 (sensory) | 0.625 | 32, 23, 22 | ~26 |
| L4-S3-M2 | 3 | 0.56 | 34, 39, 20 | ~31 |
| L4-S2-M3 | 3 | 0 | 57, 49, 47 | ~51 |

**Why holistic:** L1-S1-M2 and L1-S1-M3 each swap in one new motor rule and are otherwise identical. A part-based learner should find them equally costly, but one took about 7 examples and the other about 39. That gap is well beyond the noise between repeated tests, so it points to transfer based on similarity to the trained task. Cost also doesn't follow the new-rule count: the three-new-rule task L4-S3-M2 cost about the same as the one-new-rule tasks.

**Caveats:**
- The learner's own similarity measure isn't simply output overlap. L1-S2-M1 (0.625 overlap) and L4-S3-M2 (0.56) were no cheaper than L2-S1-M1, which has no overlap.
- The verdict rests mainly on the one contrast between M2 and M3. If the part-based learner could charge different costs for different rules, that would weaken it, but the hypothesis as stated rules that out.
